subquestions.question: Will a federal or New York City investigation into Eric Adams or his campaign announce a new indictment, subpoena, or criminal charge against a current or former campaign official between 2025-09-01 and 2025-09-25?
subquestions.background_information:
Eric Adams is running for re-election as New York City mayor amid ongoing scrutiny of his campaign and former aides. As of August 2025, two former top advisers—Winnie Greco and Ingrid Lewis-Martin—have been implicated in federal and city investigations. Greco, a former fundraiser and City Hall liaison, was caught attempting to give a reporter $120 in cash hidden in a potato chip bag on August 20, 2025, which she claimed was a cultural gesture. The incident was reported to both the New York City Department of Investigation (DOI) and federal prosecutors in Brooklyn. Greco had previously resigned in October 2024 following FBI raids linked to an investigation into possible foreign influence in Adams’s 2021 campaign. Separately, Ingrid Lewis-Martin, Adams’s former chief adviser, was indicted in August 2025 on charges of bribery, conspiracy, and money laundering by the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office. Although a federal case against Adams himself was dismissed in April 2025, the continued legal pressure on his inner circle raises concerns about further developments. Legal experts suggest that investigations often unfold in phases, and new charges or subpoenas could emerge as prosecutors build cases. Given Adams’s already strained political position—polling far behind Democratic nominee Zohran Mamdani—further legal action could increase pressure on him to drop out of the race.

The announcement must be made via an official press release, court filing, or public statement from a government official or law enforcement spokesperson. Resolution will be based on credible reporting from at least two major news outlets (e.g., The New York Times, The City, Associated Press, or Reuters) or a direct source from one of the following: U.S. Department of Justice (https://www.justice.gov), Manhattan District Attorney’s Office (https://www.manhattanda.org), New York City Department of Investigation (https://www1.nyc.gov/site/doi/index.page), or FBI New York Field Office (https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/newyork). The emergence of new charges or subpoenas against Adams’s associates could signal escalating scrutiny, increase media and public pressure, and strain campaign operations—factors that might lead Adams to reconsider his candidacy. This subquestion captures a meaningful early signal of instability that could precede a formal withdrawal, making it a high-value crux for forecasters assessing the likelihood of Adams dropping out. It is not a restatement of the ultimate question but instead focuses on a specific, observable precursor event with direct relevance to the political viability of his campaign.

evidence.step1_decompose: Required condition: Between 2025-09-01 and 2025-09-25, a federal or NYC investigative body must publicly announce a new indictment, criminal charge, or subpoena targeting a current or former official of Eric Adams's 2025 mayoral campaign. (4) Former top cop Donlon's criminal referral letter to DOJ (September 10, 2025) — REJECTED because a letter requesting investigation is not itself a charge, indictment, or subpoena. No qualifying events within September 1-25, 2025 were identified.
evidence.step4_criteria_matching: No event within the window exactly satisfies the resolution criteria. The Ingrid Lewis-Martin charges [Newsday](https://www.newsday.com/news/nation/nyc-mayor-eric-adams-corruption-investigation-y73909) and [Fox News](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/former-top-adams-adviser-donors-charged-bribery-case-cuomo-mocks-chips-stunt) occurred on August 21, 2025 — before the window. evidence.step8_final_decision: No qualifying event (new indictment, criminal charge, or subpoena against a current or former official of Eric Adams's 2025 mayoral campaign by a federal or NYC investigative body) was found within the September 1-25, 2025 window. subquestions.question: Will Taylor Swift's album 'The Life of a Showgirl' be the most-streamed album on Spotify globally for the period between 2025-10-01 and 2025-10-31?
subquestions.background_information:
Taylor Swift is set to release her 12th studio album, 'The Life of a Showgirl,' on October 3, 2025. The album has already broken Spotify's record for the most pre-saved album in the platform's history, surpassing her own previous record set by 'The Tortured Poets Department' in 2024. Given the massive pre-release momentum—including a record-breaking appearance on the 'New Heights' podcast with 1.3 million concurrent YouTube viewers—and Swift's cultural dominance in 2025, early streaming performance for 'The Life of a Showgirl' is expected to be exceptionally strong. The first four weeks post-release (October 3–31) will be a critical window for accumulating streams, and dominance during this period could signal sustained momentum necessary to become the top artist of 2025 on Spotify. As of 2024, Swift was Spotify’s most-streamed artist with over 26.6 billion global streams, and she has maintained a strong lead in cumulative streams throughout 2025.

subquestions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if Taylor Swift's album 'The Life of a Showgirl' is the most-streamed album on Spotify globally between 2025-10-01 and 2025-10-31, inclusive. evidence.step1_decompose: Condition for Yes: Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' must be the most-streamed album on Spotify globally for the period Oct 1–31, 2025, as evidenced by official Spotify data published in Spotify Wrapped (regional/global top albums), Spotify press releases, blog posts, or @Spotify/@SpotifyCharts social media. evidence.step8_final_decision: The question resolves No. While Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' dominated Spotify on its release day (Oct 3, 2025) and topped charts for multiple days, no official Spotify data was found that identifies it as the most-streamed album globally for the specific period October 1–31, 2025. These attacks were largely intercepted by Israel's multi-layered missile defense systems, but they signal a significant escalation in direct confrontation between the two nations. Iran has also provided weapons and logistical support to proxy groups such as the Houthis in Yemen, who have launched over 130 ballistic missiles and more than 150 drones at Israel since November 2023 (The Times of Israel, 2025). Iran’s military doctrine increasingly emphasizes long-range precision strike capabilities, having unveiled new drones and ballistic missiles in 2024 named after key military figures, suggesting a strategic shift toward greater regional deterrence (Wikinews, 2025). Given the high tension and recent escalations, Iranian offensive actions could serve as either a precursor to or a response that increases the likelihood of an Israeli retaliatory strike on Iranian soil.

subquestions.question: Will U.S. customs duty collections exceed $200 billion between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01, based on the Monthly Treasury Statement published by the U.S. Department of the Treasury?
subquestions.background_information:
As of July 2025, U.S. customs duty collections had reached $150 billion for the fiscal year, with record monthly collections of $27.2 billion in June and $28 billion in July. The fiscal year 2025 runs from October 1, 2024, to September 30, 2025. With $150 billion collected by the end of July, the U.S. is on a trajectory to potentially exceed $250 billion in total tariff revenue for the fiscal year. To reach $250 billion, an additional $100 billion would need to be collected in the final three months of the fiscal year, averaging about $33.3 billion per month—significantly higher than the current monthly pace. The Monthly Treasury Statement (MTS), published by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, provides official monthly data on federal receipts, including customs duties. The most recent MTS reports are publicly available and serve as the authoritative source for tracking real-time tariff collections. Reaching $200 billion by the end of September would imply a continued acceleration in collections and increase the likelihood of surpassing $250 billion by the end of the fiscal year.

Sources:
- U.S. Treasury Monthly Statement: https://www.fiscal.treasury.gov/reports-statements/monthly-statement/
- Fiscal Year 2025 Monthly Treasury Statement (July 2025): https://www.fiscal.treasury.gov/files/reports-statements/monthly-statement/mt202507.pdf
subquestions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if the cumulative U.S. customs duty collections reported in the Monthly Treasury Statement published by the U.S. Department of the Treasury for the period between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01 (inclusive) show that total collections for fiscal year 2025 exceed $200 billion. The data must be sourced from the official Monthly Treasury Statement available at https://www.fiscal.treasury.gov/reports-statements/monthly-statement/. If no statement covering the period ending September 30, 2025, is published by October 31, 2025, this question resolves to No. In the event that the reported customs duty collections fall exactly at $200 billion, the question resolves to Yes only if the value is strictly greater than $200 billion. Adjustments for refunds or retroactive changes after publication do not count; only the originally published figure as of the first release of the September 2025 MTS is valid.
subquestions.rationale: This subquestion serves as a high-value indicator for whether tariff collections are on track to exceed $250 billion in FY2025. Given that $150 billion was collected by the end of July, reaching $200 billion by the end of September would require an average of $25 billion per month over August and September—less than the $28 billion collected in July. If collections fail to reach $200 billion by the end of September, it becomes increasingly unlikely that the $250 billion threshold can be met, as it would require an unprecedented $50 billion in October alone. Thus, resolving this subquestion provides strong evidence about the plausibility of the ultimate outcome.

evidence.step1_decompose: Condition for Yes: The Monthly Treasury Statement for the period ending September 30, 2025 (FY2025 full year) must report total customs duty collections exceeding $200 billion. The statement must be published by October 31, 2025. Key entities: U.S. Treasury Department, Monthly Treasury Statement, customs duty collections, FY2025. Threshold: strictly greater than $200 billion.
evidence.step2_search_queries: Query 1: 'U.S. customs duty collections 2025 Monthly Treasury Statement fiscal year' (2025-09-01 to 2025-10-31). Query 2: 'Monthly Treasury Statement September 2025 customs duties revenue' (same period). Query 3: 'Treasury fiscal year 2025 customs duties total $202 billion annual report' (2025-10-01 to 2025-10-31). Query 4: 'Monthly Treasury Statement September 2025 published fiscal.treasury.gov'. Query 5: 'government shutdown October 2025 Treasury Monthly Statement delay publication'. Query 6: 'Treasury Department MTS September 2025 customs duties $195 billion $202 billion official release'.
evidence.step3_event_detection: Candidate events identified: (1) The Monthly Treasury Statement for FY2025 (September 2025) was released on October 16, 2025, within the October 31 deadline. (2) Multiple sources report FY2025 customs duty collections from this MTS. Key figures cited: $195 billion (net customs receipts, per official Treasury-cited sources including Yahoo Finance, Devdiscourse official release, Straits Times, Zero Hedge MTS direct citation) vs $202 billion (gross customs duties, per AFP, MarketWatch/Morningstar, yen.com.gh, Market Screener). The government shutdown (started October 1, 2025) may have delayed the MTS, but it was still published October 16, 2025 within the October 31 deadline. No event rejected for timing reasons, but there is conflicting data on the exact customs duty figure.
evidence.step4_criteria_matching: The MTS was published October 16, 2025, within the October 31 deadline. However, there is a critical conflict in reported figures: Most authoritative Treasury-referencing sources (Reuters/Yahoo Finance via Devdiscourse 'Update 2' explicitly citing the MTS as $195 billion net customs receipts; Zero Hedge explicitly citing MTS as $195 billion; Straits Times: '$195 billion in net customs receipts'; Washington Times: $195 billion; CBO: $195 billion) report $195 billion as the MTS figure for net customs receipts. Other sources (AFP October 16: '$202 billion'; Morningstar/MarketWatch: '$202 billion'; Market Screener: '$202 billion'; yen.com.gh: '$202 billion') report $202 billion as gross customs duties. The MTS contains both a 'Receipts by Source' table (showing gross receipts including customs duties) and a 'Budget Receipts' table (showing net customs). The $202 billion figure likely represents gross customs duties collected before refunds, while $195 billion is net after refunds (~$7 billion in refunds). The resolution criteria says 'total collections' which could be interpreted as either gross or net. The question appears to track 'customs duty collections' which in the MTS is typically the gross receipts line in Table 4 or the net budget receipts line. This ambiguity means I cannot definitively confirm or deny whether the $200B threshold was crossed in the 'originally published figure' from the MTS without direct access to the MTS document.
evidence.step5_timestamp_extraction: The Treasury Department's Monthly Treasury Statement for September 2025 was released on October 16, 2025. Multiple sources published on October 16-17, 2025 confirm this. The exact time within October 16 is not available from news sources.
evidence.step6_first_occurrence_check: The October 16, 2025 MTS publication is the first and only official release of the September 2025 MTS. No earlier qualifying occurrence exists as the MTS covering the period through September 30, 2025 could only be published after that date. Preliminary CBO estimates (published October 8, 2025) referenced $195 billion in customs duties but were not the MTS.
evidence.step7_verification: Contradictory evidence: The $195 billion figure is reported as 'net customs receipts' by multiple sources explicitly citing the Treasury MTS, while $202 billion is described as gross customs duties. The MTS tracks both. The Fox News article from September 2 reported that through the end of August 2025, total tariff receipts exceeded $183 billion (using 'Customs and Certain Excise Taxes' data). Adding September's ~$30 billion to the $165 billion through August (per Yahoo Finance August 11 article) gives approximately $195 billion net. However, some sources indicate September contributed $29.7 billion bringing total to $195 billion, while gross collections including refunded amounts would be approximately $202 billion. The MTS itself shows both metrics. The question asks about 'customs duty collections' which is ambiguous between gross and net. Most authoritative MTS-specific citations say $195 billion (net). The $202 billion sources appear to be using the gross receipts table from the same MTS.
evidence.step8_final_decision: The September 2025 MTS was published October 16, 2025 (within the October 31 deadline). However, there is a material conflict in reported figures: (1) The majority of sources explicitly citing the MTS report $195 billion in net customs receipts for FY2025, which is BELOW the $200 billion threshold. (2) Some sources report $202 billion in gross customs duties from the same MTS, which is ABOVE the threshold. The resolution criteria specifies 'cumulative U.S. customs duty collections' without specifying net vs. gross. Given this ambiguity, I cannot definitively determine whether the question resolves Yes or No, as it depends on which line of the MTS (gross $202B or net $195B) is the relevant metric. This constitutes conflicting evidence that cannot be definitively resolved without direct access to the MTS document. However, weighing the evidence: the majority of sources explicitly referencing the MTS as a primary source cite $195 billion as the customs duty figure from that statement, while $202 billion appears in sources that may be using a different table or methodology. The most authoritative Treasury Department direct citation (from multiple Reuters/AP-based reports) consistently says $195 billion for net customs receipts. Given this, the most likely MTS figure for 'customs duty collections' as reported is $195 billion (net), which is BELOW $200 billion, suggesting resolution as No. But the existence of multiple credible sources reporting $202 billion introduces enough uncertainty that I must consider this resolvable=false.

subquestions.question: Will the French National Assembly pass a motion of no confidence in Prime Minister François Bayrou between 2025-09-01 and 2025-09-15?
subquestions.background_information:

Bayrou’s government, formed amid a year-long political deadlock, is proposing €44 billion in budget cuts, including scrapping two public holidays and freezing public spending increases. These measures have drawn fierce opposition from both the far-right National Rally and the far-left France Unbowed, making Bayrou’s survival in office uncertain. Multiple news sources report that if Bayrou loses the confidence vote, he must resign along with his government, triggering a potential constitutional crisis. While Macron has pledged to serve his full term until 2027, a failed vote could force him to appoint a new prime minister, dissolve parliament, or face mounting pressure to resign. The outcome of this vote is a key indicator of Macron’s ability to maintain executive stability and govern effectively through the remainder of his term. A successful no-confidence motion would mark the sixth prime minister ousted during Macron’s presidency, underscoring the fragility of his administration.

subquestions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if a motion of no confidence in Prime Minister François Bayrou is passed by the French National Assembly between 2025-09-01 and 2025-09-15 (inclusive). subquestions.question: Will the Lebanese Armed Forces publicly announce the deployment of additional troops into at least three Hezbollah-dominated southern Lebanese districts (Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Marjayoun) between October 1, 2025, and October 31, 2025?

This follows a November 2024 ceasefire agreement and sustained international pressure—particularly from the U.S., France, and Gulf states—for Lebanon to assert exclusive control over its territory and armed forces, in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701. Hezbollah, however, has consistently refused to disarm while Israeli forces remain in southern Lebanon, maintaining that its weapons are essential for national defense. Recent reports indicate that the LAF has begun planning for a phased deployment into southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has historically exercised de facto military control. As of late September 2025, the LAF has not yet made a public announcement of troop movements into these areas, though U.S. and French officials have signaled support for such a move as a confidence-building step toward broader disarmament. The deployment of LAF troops into Hezbollah strongholds would be a tangible, observable indicator of the state’s attempt to reassert sovereignty and could precede or accompany negotiations on Hezbollah’s disarmament.

Conversely, a deployment could increase the probability of future negotiations or pressure on Hezbollah, making this a high-information crux for forecasters assessing the likelihood of Hezbollah’s official disarmament announcement by December 31, 2025.

subquestions.question: Will Iran expel International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors from its nuclear facilities between January 6, 2026, and February 5, 2026?
subquestions.background_information:
Since the June 2025 conflict between Israel and Iran—dubbed the '12-day war'—tensions have remained high, despite a ceasefire brokered by former U.S. President Donald Trump on June 24, 2025. During the conflict, Israel conducted extensive airstrikes on Iranian nuclear and military facilities, followed by U.S. strikes on three key nuclear sites, including Fordo and Natanz. In response, Iran significantly reduced cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), and its parliament passed legislation requiring Supreme National Security Council approval for any future IAEA access. Iranian officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, have accused the IAEA of bias and inaction, particularly for failing to condemn the Israeli and U.S. strikes. On December 29, 2025, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmael Baghaei reiterated Iran’s demand that IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi condemn the attacks, warning that continued political bias undermines the agency’s credibility. As of January 5, 2026, Iran has maintained a posture of self-reliance and heightened vigilance, suggesting a willingness to further restrict international oversight if diplomatic grievances remain unaddressed. The expulsion of IAEA inspectors would signal a major deterioration in diplomatic trust and could precede or accompany renewed military escalation, as it would indicate Iran’s rejection of international monitoring and a potential intent to accelerate nuclear activities without oversight.

Sources:
- France 24: [Looking back at Israel and Iran's '12-day war'](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20251226-looking-back-at-israel-and-iran-s-12-day-war-direct-conflict-breaks-out-between-arch-enemies)
- Trend: [Iranian spokesman paints nation's demand before IAEA](https://en.trend.az/iran/foreign-policy/3331979.html)
- Trend: [Iran affirms full compliance with its obligations under NPT - FM](https://en.trend.az/iran/foreign-policy/3328977.html)
subquestions.resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2026-01-06 and 2026-02-05 (inclusive), Iran officially expels or withdraws access for International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors from any of its nuclear facilities, as confirmed by either: (1) an official statement from the Iranian government or Supreme National Security Council; or (2) a public report from the IAEA confirming that inspectors have been barred from conducting scheduled inspections at one or more Iranian nuclear sites due to Iranian government action. 

Resolution sources:
- IAEA Official Statements: https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/press-statements
- Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs: https://en.mfa.gov.ir/
- Major international news outlets (e.g., Reuters, AP, BBC, AFP) reporting with attribution to official IAEA or Iranian government sources.

If no such expulsion or access withdrawal is confirmed during the resolution window, the question resolves No. If Iran merely restricts the scope of inspections (e.g., limiting access to certain facilities or data) without expelling inspectors or canceling scheduled visits, this does not count as a 'Yes'. If the IAEA voluntarily suspends inspections due to safety concerns or other reasons not directly caused by Iranian government action, this also does not count as a 'Yes'. If the outcome is postponed or delayed beyond the resolution window (e.g., announcement made after February 5, 2026), the question resolves No.
subquestions.rationale: The expulsion of IAEA inspectors would be a strong indicator of deteriorating diplomatic relations and a potential precursor to renewed military escalation between Iran and Israel. Such a move would signal Iran’s rejection of international oversight, possibly in preparation for advancing its nuclear program, which Israel views as an existential threat. Given Israel’s previous willingness to conduct military strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities (e.g., June 2025’s Operation Rising Lion), a loss of IAEA access could increase the likelihood of Israeli preemptive action, thereby breaking the ceasefire. This subquestion is not a restatement of the ultimate question but captures a distinct, observable diplomatic event that would significantly shift the risk landscape. It is grounded in recent developments, including Iran’s reduced cooperation with the IAEA and public grievances over the agency’s perceived bias, making it a high-value early warning signal.

evidence.step1_decompose: Required: Iran must officially expel or withdraw IAEA inspector access from nuclear facilities between Jan 6 – Feb 5, 2026. Observable evidence: official Iranian government/Supreme National Security Council statement OR IAEA public report confirming inspectors barred from scheduled inspections due to Iranian government action. Key distinction: restriction of scope (already ongoing since June 2025) does NOT qualify. Must be a NEW expulsion or withdrawal.

evidence.step8_final_decision: The resolution criteria requires a NEW expulsion or withdrawal of access WITHIN the Jan 6 – Feb 5, 2026 window. The window closed with no qualifying expulsion event. Resolution: No.

The film remained #1 through Nov 21 (confirmed by Hollywood Reporter citing Fandango data). No competing film challenged its position. Resolution: Yes, with earliest qualifying confirmation on November 13, 2025.

question: Starmer out in 2025?

subquestions.question: Will a leadership challenge against Keir Starmer be formally announced by a sitting Labour MP between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01?
subquestions.background_information:
Keir Starmer's leadership has come under increasing scrutiny in 2025 amid declining Labour Party poll numbers, poor public approval ratings, and market instability linked to fiscal policy uncertainty. A July 2025 report by Sky News highlighted 'unhappiness and despair' among senior Labour MPs, with two unnamed ministers suggesting Starmer 'might have to go in months' if performance does not improve. An Ipsos survey from the same period found 73% of UK adults were dissatisfied with Starmer’s performance—the lowest approval rating recorded for a prime minister in their first year in office. Additionally, internal party polling cited by LabourList indicated that former leader Ed Miliband was viewed more favorably than Starmer as a potential leader, raising the prospect of a leadership challenge. While no formal challenge has been announced as of mid-2025, growing discontent within the Labour Party suggests vulnerability. A formal leadership challenge would require nomination by at least 20% of Labour MPs (currently 60 out of 301), but even the announcement of such intent by a sitting MP could signal significant internal dissent and increase the likelihood of Starmer's eventual removal. 

Sources:
- Sky News report on Labour discontent: https://news.sky.com/story/labour-ministers-say-keir-starmer-might-have-to-go-in-months-13384752
- Ipsos dissatisfaction polling: https://www.ipsos.com/en/uk/keir-starmer-approval-rating-lowest-ever-recorded-first-year
- LabourList poll on leadership favourability: https://labourlist.org/2025/07/miliband-leads-labour-leadership-favourability-poll-as-starmer-rating-drops/
subquestions.resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01 (inclusive), a sitting Labour Member of Parliament (MP) publicly announces support for or intention to initiate a formal leadership challenge against Keir Starmer as Leader of the Labour Party. A 'formal announcement' includes a public statement via press release, media interview, social media post (e.g., X, Facebook, or official website), or parliamentary speech explicitly stating that the MP believes a leadership contest should occur or that they intend to trigger one. The announcement must name Starmer as the current leader under challenge. 

Resolution will be determined by credible media reporting from at least two independent, reputable news outlets (e.g., BBC News, The Guardian, Sky News, Financial Times) or an official statement from the UK Labour Party. 

If no such announcement occurs during the specified period, the question resolves No. 

In the event that the announcement is made but later retracted, the question still resolves Yes if the initial statement met the criteria. 

If the data source becomes unavailable, resolution will be based on a consensus of reliable reporting from major UK news organizations. 

Examples of resolving Yes: 
- On September 15, 2025, Labour MP Zara Khan gives a BBC interview stating, 'I will be submitting a nomination for a leadership contest because Keir Starmer is no longer the right leader for our party.' 

Examples of not resolving Yes: 
- A Labour MP criticizes Starmer’s policies but does not mention a leadership challenge. 
- A former Labour MP (no longer sitting) calls for Starmer to step down. 

Sources for resolution: 
- BBC News: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news 
- The Guardian: https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news 
- Sky News: https://news.sky.com 
- Financial Times: https://www.ft.com
subquestions.rationale: A formal leadership challenge announcement by a sitting Labour MP would be a strong early indicator of internal party instability and could significantly increase the likelihood of Starmer ceasing to be Prime Minister before the end of 2025. Given that leadership challenges in the UK Labour Party require significant parliamentary support, even a single public announcement would signal growing dissent and could catalyze broader momentum. This subquestion is distinct from the ultimate question (which concerns actual removal from office) but serves as a meaningful precursor event—historically, public leadership challenges often precede resignation or removal, especially when paired with low approval and poor electoral performance. It is also time-sensitive and grounded in current political dynamics, making it a high-value information signal for forecasters assessing Starmer’s tenure.

evidence.step1_decompose: Condition for Yes: A sitting Labour MP must publicly announce (via press release, media interview, social media, or parliamentary speech) their support for or intention to initiate a formal leadership challenge against Keir Starmer as Labour leader, explicitly stating that a leadership contest should occur or they intend to trigger one, with the announcement naming Starmer. Observable evidence: credible reporting from 2+ reputable outlets (BBC, Guardian, Sky News, FT) within Sept 1–Oct 1 2025. Key entities: sitting Labour MP (not a mayor, peer, or former MP), formal announcement of contest, Keir Starmer named.
evidence.step2_search_queries: 1) 'Labour MP leadership challenge Keir Starmer 2025' (Sept–Oct window) — to find any formal announcements; 2) 'Starmer leadership contest Labour Party September 2025' — to find formal contest triggers; 3) 'Labour MP formally announces leadership challenge Starmer nomination September 2025' — to find specific formal nominations; 4) 'Clive Lewis Rosena Allin-Khan Richard Burgon leadership challenge Starmer resign' — to check specific MPs; 5) 'Labour leadership contest triggered formal nomination September October 2025' — to find triggered contests; 6) 'Andy Burnham MP leadership challenge Starmer formal announcement contest' — to check Burnham status; 7) '"leadership challenge" "leadership contest" Labour MP announce trigger formal Starmer' — to find formal announcements
evidence.step3_event_detection: Candidate events identified: (1) Richard Burgon (sitting MP) said Starmer's removal is 'inevitable' if May elections go badly — conditional prediction, not a formal challenge announcement; (2) Clive Lewis (sitting MP) called Starmer 'not up to the job' and 'called for Starmer to step down' per New Statesman — this is criticism and a call to resign, not a formal challenge announcement; (3) Andy Burnham confirmed MPs urged him to run and said he'd 'play any role' — Burnham is NOT a sitting MP (he is Mayor of Greater Manchester), so fails the criteria; (4) No article from any reputable source reports an actual formal leadership challenge being triggered by a sitting Labour MP during this window. The Labour conference (Sept 28–Oct 1) passed with Starmer delivering his keynote on Sept 30 with no formal challenge having been launched.
evidence.step4_criteria_matching: No event exactly matches the resolution criteria. The closest events are: Clive Lewis calling Starmer 'not up to the job' ([North Norfolk News](https://www.northnorfolknews.co.uk/news/25463708.norwich-mp-clive-lewis-says-sir-keir-starmer-not-job/)) and per New Statesman 'calling for Starmer to step down' — but calling for a resignation is distinct from announcing support for or intention to initiate a formal leadership contest. Richard Burgon's prediction that Starmer 'will be gone' after May elections ([Yahoo/The Independent](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/keir-starmer-richard-burgon-labour-mp-mandelson-b2826527.html)) is a conditional future prediction, not a formal announcement of a current challenge. Andy Burnham is not a sitting MP. Multiple sources ([The Independent](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/politics-explained/labour-leadership-challenge-keir-starmer-andy-burnham-b2827742.html), [The Conversation](http://theconversation.com/andy-burnhams-leadership-ambitions-what-is-the-path-to-mounting-a-challenge-against-keir-starmer-266160)) explicitly analyzed whether a challenge was feasible and concluded it was unlikely/improbable in the near term.
evidence.step5_timestamp_extraction: No exact timestamp of a qualifying formal announcement could be extracted, because no such qualifying announcement was identified in the evidence.
evidence.step6_first_occurrence_check: No qualifying occurrence found in the window Sept 1–Oct 1, 2025.
evidence.step7_verification: Contradictory evidence checked: Starmer delivered his conference keynote on Sept 30, 2025, still as Labour leader ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/keir-starmer-labour-party-conference-speech-farage-2788160fd8cc084c7f032c46a5a31776)), with speculation about future challenges but no formal contest triggered. Multiple articles frame any leadership challenge as a future possibility (after May 2026 elections) rather than a current formal challenge. The inews.co.uk article explicitly explains that a formal Labour leadership contest can only be triggered if the leader resigns or the post is declared vacant — there is no mechanism for MPs to unilaterally 'trigger' a contest by announcing support. This means the concept of 'formally announcing intention to trigger a contest' is largely aspirational/rhetorical within Labour's rules. No retraction evidence to consider. No conflicting evidence suggesting a formal challenge was made.
evidence.step8_final_decision: The window closed (Oct 1, 2025) with no sitting Labour MP having made a formal announcement meeting the resolution criteria. While there was significant intra-party criticism, calls for resignation, and speculation about leadership challenges, no sitting Labour MP formally announced they believed a leadership contest should occur NOW or that they intended to trigger one during the Sept 1–Oct 1 window. Andy Burnham (the most prominent figure positioning for a future challenge) is not a sitting MP. Clive Lewis and Richard Burgon made critical statements but did not formally announce a leadership contest. Resolution: No.

question: Bank of Japan decreases interest rates after January 2026 meeting?
description:
The Statement on Monetary Policy for the Bank of Japan's Monetary Policy meeting for January is scheduled to be released on January 23, 2026 (https://www.boj.or.jp/en/mopo/mpmsche_minu/index.htm).

This market will resolve to the amount of basis points the upper bound of the short-term policy interest rate is changed by versus the level it was prior to the Bank of Japan's January 2026 meeting.

If the short-term policy interest rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded up to the nearest 25 and will resolve to the relevant bracket. (e.g. if there's a cut/increase of 12.5 bps it will be considered to be 25 bps)

The primary resolution source for this market will be the official website of the Bank of Japan (https://www.boj.or.jp/en/mopo/mpmsche_minu/index.htm), however a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

This market may resolve as soon as the Bank of Japan's statement for their January meeting with relevant data is issued. If no statement is released by the end date of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the "No change" bracket.

subquestions.question: Will the Bank of Japan issue a statement or hold a press conference between 2025-11-08 and 2025-12-08 indicating that inflation expectations have reached or exceeded 2% and that wage growth is sufficient to sustainably achieve the price stability target?
subquestions.background_information:
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has maintained its short-term policy rate at 0.5% since January 2025, when it exited its decade-long negative interest rate policy. The central bank has consistently stated that further rate hikes depend on whether inflation expectations are durably anchored at 2% and whether wage growth is strong enough to sustain price increases without eroding household purchasing power. Recent data shows Japan’s core CPI has remained at or above 2% for over three years, and the BOJ revised its fiscal 2025–2026 growth forecast to 0.7% in October 2025. However, Governor Kazuo Ueda has emphasized caution, noting that 'inflation expectations aren’t yet at the 2% level' and citing uncertainty around U.S. trade policy and its impact on wages. Two board members dissented in favor of a rate hike in September and October, signaling growing internal support for tightening. A key signal ahead of the January 2026 meeting will be whether the BOJ shifts its forward guidance to reflect greater confidence in sustained inflation and wage growth—conditions widely seen as prerequisites for further rate hikes. The BOJ typically communicates such shifts through its quarterly outlook reports, press conferences, or ad hoc statements.

Sources:
- BOJ maintains rate at 0.5%, cites need for caution on inflation expectations: https://www.boj.or.jp/en/mopo/press/2025/20251030a.pdf
- Dissent grows within BOJ board over timing of next rate hike: https://www.reuters.com/markets/asia/bank-of-japan-holds-rates-unchanged-two-members-favour-hike-2025-10-30/
- BOJ revises growth forecast upward amid solid consumption: https://www.boj.or.jp/en/research/papers/2025/25e10a.pdf
subquestions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-11-08 and 2025-12-08 (inclusive), the Bank of Japan issues an official statement, holds a press conference, or releases a report in which a senior BOJ official (Governor, Deputy Governor, or Policy Board member) explicitly states that inflation expectations have reached or exceeded 2% and that wage growth is sufficient to sustainably achieve the 2% price stability target. The statement must be made in an official capacity and published on the BOJ’s official website (https://www.boj.or.jp/en/) or reported by at least two credible financial news outlets (e.g., Reuters, Bloomberg, Nikkei Asia, Financial Times) with direct quotes from the official source. If no such statement is made during the resolution window, the question resolves No. If the BOJ makes a statement that only partially meets the criteria (e.g., mentions inflation expectations at 2% but expresses doubt about wage growth), it does not count. In the event the BOJ website becomes inaccessible, resolution will be based on consensus reporting from the aforementioned credible outlets.
subquestions.rationale: This subquestion is a strong indicator of the BOJ’s evolving stance ahead of the January 2026 meeting. A public acknowledgment that inflation expectations have reached 2% and that wage growth is sufficient would signal growing consensus within the central bank for further tightening, increasing the likelihood of a rate hike or hawkish shift in January. Conversely, continued expressions of caution would suggest a hold is more likely. This question captures a meaningful shift in forward guidance—something forecasters can observe before the actual rate decision—making it a high-value crux for the ultimate question of whether the BOJ decreases (or increases) rates after January 2026. It avoids simply restating the ultimate question by focusing on a specific, observable communication event that precedes the policy action.

evidence.step1_decompose: Requires: A senior BOJ official (Governor, Deputy Governor, or Policy Board member) explicitly stating BOTH (1) inflation expectations have reached or exceeded 2% AND (2) wage growth is sufficient to sustainably achieve the 2% price stability target. Must be in an official capacity, in the resolution window 2025-11-08 to 2025-12-08, published on boj.or.jp/en/ or reported by at least two credible outlets with direct quotes.
evidence.step2_search_queries: Query 1: 'Bank of Japan inflation expectations 2% wage growth price stability target 2025' (Nov 8 - Dec 8). Query 2: 'BOJ Governor Ueda press conference statement inflation wages November December 2025'. Query 3: 'BOJ inflation expectations reached 2% wage growth sufficient statement November 2025'. Query 4: 'Bank of Japan Noguchi inflation expectations stabilized wage growth sufficient December 2025'. Query 5: 'BOJ policy board member inflation expectations anchored 2% December 2025'. Query 6: 'Bank of Japan statement wage growth sufficient price stability sustainably achieve 2025'.
evidence.step3_event_detection: Candidate events found: (1) Noguchi Nov 27 speech - explicitly stated inflation expectations have NOT stabilized at 2%, rejected. (2) Ueda Nov 13 parliament - said inflation 'gradually accelerating toward' 2% target, not yet reached, rejected. (3) Ueda Nov 21 parliament - said more data on wages needed, rejected. (4) Ueda Dec 1 Nagoya press conference - gathering wage data ahead of December meeting, acknowledged conditions not yet fully confirmed, rejected. (5) BOJ Oct meeting summary released Nov 10 - one member said conditions 'almost' met, not explicitly met, rejected. No candidate event satisfies both criteria simultaneously.
evidence.step4_criteria_matching: None of the BOJ statements in the window explicitly state that inflation expectations have REACHED OR EXCEEDED 2%. [Noguchi Nov 27](https://www.morningstar.com/news/dow-jones/202511268358/boj-rate-hikes-must-proceed-with-caution-board-member-says) explicitly stated 'inflation expectations have yet to stabilize at 2%'. [Ueda Nov 13](https://www.actionforex.com/live-comments/619077-bojs-ueda-highlights-tight-job-market-resilient-consumption/) said inflation is 'gradually accelerating toward our 2% target' — not reached. [Ueda Dec 1](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/rate-hikes-wouldn-t-put-brakes-on-japan-s-economy-boj-s-ueda-says-update-ce7d51dbd08bf52d) said still gathering wage data. No statement satisfies Condition 1 or Condition 2.
evidence.step5_timestamp_extraction: No qualifying event exists, so no timestamp can be extracted. The evidence explicitly shows BOJ officials stated the opposite — that both conditions had NOT yet been met during the window.
evidence.step6_first_occurrence_check: No qualifying occurrence of the combined conditions was found at any point in the resolution window.
evidence.step7_verification: The evidence is consistent across multiple sources: Noguchi (Nov 27) explicitly stated inflation expectations have not stabilized at 2%; Ueda (Nov 13, Nov 21, Dec 1) consistently indicated underlying inflation is still moving toward the target, not at it, and that wage data is still being collected. The BOJ's own projection places underlying inflation reaching 2% 'in the latter half of fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027' — a future target. No contradictory evidence found suggesting any BOJ official made the required explicit dual statement.
evidence.step8_final_decision: The question resolves No. No BOJ official explicitly stated that inflation expectations had reached or exceeded 2% AND that wage growth was sufficient to sustainably achieve the price stability target during the resolution window. In fact, BOJ officials explicitly stated the opposite — that inflation expectations had not yet stabilized at 2% and that more wage data was still needed. The window closed on December 8, 2025 without the required statement being made.

question: Will Trump's approval rating hit 40% in 2025?
description:

Note that the approval ratings for this date must be finalized before it is considered for this market (namely once the next data point is available, the previous one is finalized).

This market's resolution source will be Silver Bulletin' approval rating poll aggregator, https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin, specifically the approval rating indicated by the green trend line for the resolution date. Changes in the methodology by which Silver Bulletin calculates the approval rating will have no bearing on the resolution of this market. If Silver Bulletin's approval rating becomes permanently unavailable, RealClearPolitics will be used.

If the approval rating for December 31 is not published by January 4, 2026, 12:00 PM ET (noon), this market will resolve according to all previous datapoints.

subquestions.question: Will Donald Trump's average weekly approval rating according to Silver Bulletin's green trend line be at or above 42% for any week between September 1, 2025, and October 1, 2025?
subquestions.background_information:
As of mid-August 2025, Donald Trump's approval rating has stabilized around a net disapproval of approximately -8.5 to -8.9 percentage points, with about 45.8% approval and 55% disapproval according to Silver Bulletin's polling average. This represents a plateau after a decline in April and May, during which his approval dipped into the low 40s (e.g., 41% in a CNN poll). While there was a slight rebound in late May (net approval rising to -5.8), the trend has since flattened. Recent polling suggests that Trump remains underwater in net approval, with strong disapproval (41–42%) consistently outpacing strong approval (27–28%). The last time Trump’s approval was near or above 42% was in late May 2025. Given that the ultimate question asks whether his approval will reach 40% in 2025, a short-term indicator of momentum—such as a weekly average reaching 42%—could signal a positive trend that makes hitting 40% more likely (or conversely, sustained sub-42% readings could indicate stagnation). A 42% weekly threshold is meaningful because it represents a modest improvement from current levels and could reflect early signs of recovery in public perception.

Sources:
- Silver Bulletin: https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin
- NYMag on May 2025 stabilization: https://nymag.com/intelligencer/2025/05/trump-approval-polls-may-2025.html
- Newsweek on August 2025 ratings: https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-approval-rating-nate-silver-2025-2527893
subquestions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if Donald Trump's weekly average approval rating, as indicated by the green trend line on Silver Bulletin's approval rating tracker (https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin), is at or above 42% for any seven-day period that falls entirely within the window from 2025-09-01 to 2025-10-01. The weekly average must be derived from the daily green trend line values published during that week and must be visible and finalized on the Silver Bulletin page by October 2, 2025. If Silver Bulletin ceases publication or removes historical data, the fallback source is RealClearPolitics' Trump approval average (https://www.realclearpolling.com/approval-ratings/president/trump). If no data is available from either source, the question resolves as No. This question resolves based on data published between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01, inclusive.
subquestions.rationale: This subquestion serves as an early momentum indicator for Trump’s approval trajectory. If his weekly average reaches 42% in September 2025, it suggests positive movement in public opinion, increasing the likelihood that his approval could dip down to or below 40% later in the year (note: the ultimate question resolves positively if approval is *equal to or below* 40%, indicating the user likely meant *equal to or above* 40%; however, we interpret the intent as tracking whether approval reaches 40% in either direction). Conversely, if approval remains below 42% throughout September, it signals continued stagnation or decline, making a rebound to 40% less likely. The threshold is set at 42%—slightly above current levels—to filter out noise and capture meaningful shifts. The September timeframe provides timely insight while allowing for observable changes post-summer political lull.

evidence.step1_decompose: Condition for Yes: Silver Bulletin's green trend line (approval percentage) must be at or above 42% for any seven-day period falling entirely within Sept 1 – Oct 1, 2025. Key threshold: 42% approval (not net approval). The green trend line is Silver Bulletin's smoothed aggregate of all polls.
evidence.step2_search_queries: 1) 'Trump approval rating Silver Bulletin September 2025' — to find direct Silver Bulletin data points; 2) 'Trump approval rating September 2025 weekly average' — to find weekly approval data; 3) 'Silver Bulletin Trump approval rating trend line 42 percent September 2025' — to find if 42% threshold was discussed; 4) 'Nate Silver approval tracker Trump 44% 43% 42% September 2025' — to find specific percentage readings; 5) 'Silver Bulletin Trump approval rating green line September 1 2025' — to find earliest qualifying period data.
evidence.step3_event_detection: Multiple news sources report Silver Bulletin approval ratings throughout September 2025: Sept 5 = 44.1% approval; Sept 8 = implied ~44.5% (net -6.9); Sept 10 = 44.2% approval; Sept 14 = implied ~44% (net -7.6); Sept 19 = 44.2%; Sept 22 = 45% approval; Sept 26 = 44% approval; Sept 29 = 43.7% approval. All are well above 42%.
evidence.step4_criteria_matching: Silver Bulletin's tracker consistently showed Trump approval above 42% throughout September 2025. Specifically: on Sept 5, Nate Silver reported '44.1% approval and 51.7% disapproval' [NJ.com/600wmtradio]; on Sept 10, 'net approval stands at -7.4, with 51.6% disapproving and 44.2% approving' [The Conversation]; on Sept 19, '44.2% approval' [Twin Cities/Cook Political Report]; on Sept 22, '45% favorable and 52% unfavorable' [Democrat and Chronicle]; on Sept 26, '44% approval and 53% disapproval' [Newsweek]; on Sept 29, '43.7% who approve' [The Conversation]. All values exceed the 42% threshold throughout the entire window.
evidence.step5_timestamp_extraction: First qualifying period: The week of Sept 1-7, 2025. Silver Bulletin showed 44.1% approval on approximately Sept 5, 2025 (reported in article dated 2025-09-05 by NJ.com). The earliest clear data point within the window is from September 5, 2025.
evidence.step6_first_occurrence_check: The first qualifying occurrence is the first seven-day period starting September 1, 2025, as Silver Bulletin's approval rating was already above 44% at the start of the window (Sept 5 = 44.1%, which reflects the trend for the surrounding days). No evidence suggests approval was below 42% at any point during September 2025.
evidence.step7_verification: Contradictory evidence checked: No source reports Silver Bulletin's approval falling to or below 42% during September 2025. Even at its lowest point (late September, ~43.7%), the tracker remained well above 42%. The net approval varied between approximately -6.9 and -9.4, consistently implying approval in the 43-45% range throughout the month. Multiple independent sources (Newsweek, The Conversation, NJ.com, Democrat and Chronicle, Twin Cities) all corroborate Silver Bulletin figures above 44% throughout September 2025.
evidence.step8_final_decision: Silver Bulletin's approval tracker (green trend line) consistently showed Trump's approval between approximately 43.7% and 45% throughout all of September 2025, well above the 42% threshold required for Yes resolution. Multiple independent sources confirm these figures. The question resolves Yes, with the first qualifying occurrence being the week of September 1-7, 2025, when Silver Bulletin showed approximately 44.1% approval.

question: Will Hamas agree to disarm by December 31?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if Hamas officially announces it will disarm in the Gaza Strip by December 31, 2025, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

Only credible announcements, for example by the widely acknowledged leadership of Hamas, will qualify.

For the purposes of this market, "disarm" refers to a public commitment to relinquish or dismantle its military, whether partially or completely, in the Gaza Strip.

Announcements of partial disarmament (e.g., surrendering a class of weapons or agreeing to disarm in stages or a certain region) will qualify as long as it is part of an acknowledged disarmament process.

Only official announcements will qualify. Informal statements, plans contingent on future conditions, statements of intent without a formal policy directive, or any other statements that do not constitute a formal policy announcement will not be considered.

Primary resolution sources will include official statements from Hamas leadership; however, a wide consensus of credible reporting confirming a policy of disarmament has been instituted will also qualify.

subquestions.question: Will a senior Hamas official publicly state that Hamas is willing to enter negotiations on the specifics of disarmament in Gaza between November 30, 2025, and December 29, 2025?
subquestions.background_information:
As of late November 2025, Hamas has maintained a firm public stance against disarmament unless it is part of a broader political settlement leading to an independent Palestinian state and the end of Israeli occupation. On November 26, 2025, Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem reiterated that disarmament must be resolved through 'internal Palestinian dialogue' and national consensus, not as a precondition imposed by external actors (Arutz Sheva, 2025). However, there are indications of internal divisions and diplomatic maneuvering. Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani stated that Qatar is pressuring Hamas to accept disarmament and believes the group may be ready to relinquish governance of Gaza, though not necessarily its weapons (Arutz Sheva, 2025). Meanwhile, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have claimed that Hamas agreed to disarm as part of the Trump 20-point plan, while Hamas officials like Osama Hamdan deny this, asserting they only accepted the first phase involving a ceasefire and hostage release (Gatestone Institute, 2025). This disconnect suggests that while Hamas leadership publicly rejects disarmament, behind-the-scenes discussions may be more flexible. A public willingness to negotiate the specifics of disarmament—such as scope, verification, sequencing, or linkage to Israeli withdrawal—would represent a significant shift from outright refusal and could signal a strategic pivot toward compliance with the ultimate requirement of the peace plan. Given that the ultimate question hinges on an official announcement of disarmament by December 31, 2025, an intermediate step of entering formal negotiations on disarmament terms would be a strong leading indicator of such a decision.

Sources:
- Arutz Sheva: https://www.arutzsheva.co.il/en/news/articles/554238
- Gatestone Institute: https://www.gatestoneinstitute.org/hamas-trump-administration
- The Boston Globe: https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/10/08/world/hamas-disarmament-talks/
subquestions.resolution_criteria:
This question resolves Yes if, between 2025-11-30 and 2025-12-29, a senior Hamas official (defined as a member of the Political Bureau, the Military Wing leadership, or an officially designated spokesperson) makes a public statement indicating that Hamas is willing to enter negotiations on the specifics of disarmament in Gaza. Public statements include press conferences, official social media posts, interviews with verified media outlets, or written communiqués released by Hamas-affiliated channels such as Al-Aqsa TV or the official Hamas website (hamas.ps). The statement must go beyond reiterating conditional or principled positions (e.g., 'disarmament only after statehood') and must explicitly express openness to discussing the modalities, timeline, verification mechanisms, or scope of disarmament as part of a negotiated process. Statements that merely reaffirm past positions, reject disarmament, or defer the issue to Palestinian unity talks without signaling new openness to negotiation do not qualify.

Resolution will be based on credible, contemporaneous reporting from at least two internationally recognized news organizations (e.g., Reuters, AFP, BBC, Al Jazeera, The New York Times, or Associated Press) or direct verification from the official Hamas communication channels. If no such statement is made during the resolution window, the question resolves No.

In the event that the primary sources become unavailable, secondary confirmation via archived versions on the Wayback Machine (https://web.archive.org) or official transcripts from international mediators (Qatar, Egypt, or the UN) may be used. If the event is postponed or delayed beyond the resolution window, it does not count. The question is not contingent on the outcome of any negotiations, only on the public expression of willingness to engage in them.

Primary sources for resolution:
- Hamas official website: https://www.hamas.ps
- Al-Aqsa TV: https://www.al-aqsatv.ps
- Reuters: https://www.reuters.com
- Associated Press: https://apnews.com
subquestions.rationale: This subquestion serves as a meaningful early indicator of Hamas’s trajectory toward the ultimate outcome of agreeing to disarm by December 31, 2025. Given Hamas’s consistent public rejection of disarmament, a shift to expressing willingness to negotiate the specifics would represent a significant softening of position and a necessary precursor to any formal disarmament announcement. It helps distinguish between a static refusal and a potential strategic pivot. The question is not a restatement of the ultimate question but focuses on a distinct, observable behavioral change—engagement in negotiation—that has high informational value and is time-bound within the critical window preceding the final deadline.

subquestions.question: Will Larry Ellison's net worth increase by at least $20 billion between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index?
subquestions.background_information:

However, Musk’s wealth has been highly volatile due to Tesla stock fluctuations, including a $71.2 billion decline in early 2025 linked to political and regulatory pressures (Benzinga, 2025). In contrast, Ellison’s wealth trajectory has been more stable and upward, benefiting from AI-driven demand for cloud infrastructure. If this trend accelerates, Ellison could close the gap significantly by the end of 2025. A $20 billion increase in his net worth over a one-month window would signal strong momentum that could position him to overtake Musk before 2026, especially if Tesla continues to face headwinds.

subquestions.rationale: Larry Ellison is one of the few individuals realistically positioned to overtake Elon Musk in net worth before 2026, given his recent strong gains and lower exposure to the political and market volatility affecting Tesla. A $20 billion increase in Ellison's wealth over a one-month period would indicate an accelerating trend that could close the ~$130 billion gap with Musk within a few months, especially if Tesla's stock remains stagnant or declines. This subquestion serves as a leading indicator of whether Musk's lead is eroding due to relative wealth growth among top contenders. Forecasters who believe Musk will lose the top spot may expect strong upward momentum in Ellison’s wealth, while those expecting Musk to retain #1 may anticipate flat or declining growth for Ellison. evidence.step1_decompose: Required condition: Larry Ellison's net worth as reported by Bloomberg Billionaires Index must increase by ≥$20 billion between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01 (inclusive). The $88.5 billion surge on September 10 established a massive gain that was partially retained (net ~$60-79 billion above the September 1 level) through October 1. The resolution criteria specifies Bloomberg as primary source, with Forbes as fallback. While explicit Bloomberg October 1 data wasn't found, Forbes October 1 data (~$350 billion) confirms a massive increase. The resolution criteria also states Forbes is an accepted fallback source.
evidence.step8_final_decision: Larry Ellison's net worth increased by approximately $60-80 billion between September 1, 2025 (~$270-289 billion) and October 1, 2025 (~$350 billion), driven primarily by Oracle's massive earnings-driven stock surge on September 10. This increase far exceeds the $20 billion threshold. While direct Bloomberg Billionaires Index figures for both specific dates were not simultaneously available, the Forbes Billionaires data (an accepted fallback per resolution criteria) confirms the start (~$270.9B on Sept 1) and end (~$350B on Oct 1) values. The difference of ~$79 billion is unambiguously above $20 billion. Resolution: Yes.

The competition begins on Friday, September 26, with four foursomes (alternate shot) matches in the morning, followed by four four-ball matches in the afternoon. Each match is worth one point, with a half-point awarded to each team in the event of a tie. A total of 28 points are available, and a team needs 14.5 points to win the Cup outright. If the match ends in a 14–14 tie, Team Europe retains the Cup as the defending champion. The U.S. team, captained by Keegan Bradley, includes top players such as Scottie Scheffler, Xander Schauffele, and Bryson DeChambeau. Europe, led by captain Luke Donald, features Rory McIlroy, Jon Rahm, and Viktor Hovland. Early momentum in the Ryder Cup is often considered critical, particularly in the foursomes format, which requires strong team coordination and strategic play. Historically, winning the Friday foursomes has correlated with overall success: since 1979, the team that has won the Friday morning session has gone on to win the Cup about 70% of the time (based on historical trends). The U.S. has a strong record in home Ryder Cups, having won 4 of the last 5 on home soil. However, Europe won the last edition in 2023 at Marco Simone Golf & Country Club in Italy, and many analysts consider them resilient under pressure. The outcome of the early sessions, especially the foursomes, may indicate which team gains early control and psychological advantage.

His son, Masoud Khamenei, has reportedly taken over day-to-day operations of the Supreme Leader’s office, a significant delegation of authority (News.com.au, Breitbart, 2026-01-25–26). Since then, there has been no confirmed visual or audio appearance of Khamenei. Given his advanced age and history of health issues—including a reported prostate cancer diagnosis in 2014—his absence raises concerns about his ability to govern (BBC, 2014: https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-27174124). The Iranian regime has a history of concealing leadership health crises; for example, Ayatollah Khomeini’s death was not announced for hours after it occurred. Therefore, the presence or absence of a verified public appearance by Khamenei serves as a key indicator of his continued active control over the regime. A public appearance would signal stability and continuity, while continued absence could indicate declining health, incapacitation, or preparations for succession—all of which increase the likelihood of his eventual removal or departure before March 31, 2026.

If no such appearance is confirmed by these sources within the timeframe, the question resolves No. If official Iranian sources claim an appearance but it is widely disputed or unverified by international media, the question resolves No. If the relevant data sources become unavailable, resolution will be based on archived versions via the Wayback Machine (https://archive.org/web/) or alternative credible reporting.

subquestions.question: Will the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) close above 40 on at least one trading day between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01?
subquestions.background_information:
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), often referred to as the 'fear gauge,' measures the market's expectation of 30-day volatility in the S&P 500 Index. Elevated VIX levels are strongly correlated with periods of market stress and are often precursors to sharp equity market declines. Historically, VIX readings above 40 have coincided with extreme investor fear and have frequently preceded or accompanied marketwide circuit breaker events. For example, during the March 2020 market turmoil when multiple circuit breakers were triggered, the VIX spiked above 80. More recently, in April 2025, amid tariff-related sell-offs, the VIX rose above 35 as the S&P 500 dropped nearly 6% in a single session, approaching but not reaching the 7% threshold for a Level 1 circuit breaker (Barrons, 2025-04-03). As of late August 2025, the VIX has averaged around 20, indicating moderate volatility. A sustained move above 40 would signal a significant deterioration in market sentiment and could indicate heightened risk of a circuit breaker being triggered later in 2025.

Sources:
- Barrons: https://www.barrons.com/articles/stocks-are-in-freefall-heres-when-circuit-breakers-kick-in-4d5a7e8a
- Yahoo! Finance: https://finance.yahoo.com/news/what-is-a-circuit-breaker-heres-when-trading-is-halted-during-intense-sell-offs-180000555.html
- Cboe VIX methodology: https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/vix/
subquestions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) closes at or above 40 on any trading day between 2025-09-01 and 2025-10-01 (inclusive). The closing value is defined as the official settlement value of the VIX, as published by Cboe Global Markets at the end of each trading day. The primary source for resolution is the official VIX data available on the Cboe website: https://www.cboe.com/indices/volatility/vix/. If the Cboe website is unavailable or discontinues publication, secondary sources include Bloomberg Terminal (ticker: VIX), Yahoo Finance (https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5EVIX), or the Wall Street Journal market data section (https://www.wsj.com/market-data/quotes/index/SPX/vix). If no source reports a closing value above 40 during the resolution window, the question resolves No. If trading is halted on the Cboe or the VIX is not calculated for any reason during the window, the most recent available closing value will be used. If the event is postponed or delayed beyond the resolution window, the question will resolve based on data within the window. This question is not contingent on the cause of volatility, only the closing level of the VIX.
subquestions.rationale: A VIX close above 40 is a strong indicator of extreme market fear and elevated risk of a sharp, broad-based selloff in equities. Since marketwide circuit breakers are triggered by rapid declines in the S&P 500, conditions that produce a VIX spike are often the same conditions that could lead to a circuit breaker event. Therefore, observing such a volatility spike in September 2025 would increase the likelihood that the market is entering a period of instability, thereby increasing the probability of a circuit breaker being triggered before year-end. This subquestion provides early evidence of systemic stress without directly restating the ultimate question, and it is time-bound to a period that is informative but not determinative of the full-year outcome.
